# Notes on Acts 6 for the verse-by-verse commentary

**What I couldn't find.** I found nothing on these sites linking Acts 6 to prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. I also found nothing from Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org) or from pneumareview.com or samstorms.org. I didn't read the NET Bible notes directly; the one NET note below comes secondhand through bible.org. I could only partly see Wesley's notes on Acts 6. All of these are left out below.

**Where traditions really differ:**
- **Were the seven "deacons"?** (vv. 3, 5, 6)
- **Who chose and appointed them?** (v. 3)
- **What did laying on hands do?** (v. 6)

---

**v. 1**
- **Who the two groups were.** Guzik: the "Hebrews" were Jews who held to Jewish culture, mostly from Judea. The "Hellenists" were Jews who leaned toward Greek culture, mostly from abroad. Both groups were Christians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **The difference was mainly language.** Constable: Hebrews could speak a Semitic language and Hellenists could not. He notes that Paul counted himself a Hebrew even though he grew up outside Palestine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Satan's tactic.** Guzik sees an attempt to "divide and conquer," using old suspicion between the groups. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **The neglect was probably not deliberate.** Guzik cites Stott (more likely poor administration) and MacArthur (some needs were bound to be missed in so large a church). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **A guess about the background.** Guzik suggests the temple authorities, who normally ran help for the needy, may have stopped caring for Christian widows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **Jewish practice.** Constable: caring for widows was a priority in Judaism, and synagogues gave to widows and the poor weekly. He also notes that the complaint arose because of the widows, not among them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html

**v. 2**
- **Not pride.** Guzik says this probably wasn't a superior attitude in the apostles; it was wise delegation. He adds that a pastor who thinks such work is beneath him has something wrong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **What "tables" means.** Guzik (citing Ogilvie) and Constable (citing Longenecker) both say "serving tables" probably meant organising money and supplies, not literally waiting at tables. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Not a lower task.** Constable cites Marshall: serving tables isn't lesser work. The point is that the Twelve were specifically called to witness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html

**v. 3**
- **Qualifications.** Guzik: the men were to be both spiritually minded and practically minded. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/ Constable: the requirements are character traits, not talents. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Why seven?** Guzik suggests perhaps one man for each day of the week. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/ Other suggestions on Bible Hub: seven tables to supply, or seven as the number of completeness. Some churches, including Rome for centuries, later kept exactly seven deacons. https://biblehub.com/acts/6-3.htm Constable notes a Jewish custom of seven respected men managing public business. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Difference: who decides?**
  - Guzik (enduringword): the final decision rested with the apostles, and this was not congregational government. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
  - A commentary quoted on StudyLight (author not named): the people choose and the apostles ordain, since the people knew the candidates' reputations better. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-5.html
  - The Biblical Illustrator: this is "constitutional government," with power not wholly in the people's hands. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-5.html
  - Constable: many churches copy this pattern today, with the congregation nominating deacons and the elders appointing them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **"Men" and deacon gender.** A bible.org study says the text gives no biblical reason for choosing only men and is neutral on whether deacons must be men. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-6-9

**v. 4**
- **Prayer as well as preaching.** Guzik quotes Calvin: pastors haven't done their whole duty just by teaching each day. Guzik also stresses how much energy real preaching and prayer take. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **Prayer is the key.** Constable, citing Hiebert, calls prayer the main way God's people secure His working, and the secret of the early church's strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html

**v. 5**
- **Greek names.** All seven have Greek names, so they were probably Hellenists. Choosing them showed sensitivity to the group that complained. Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/ Gill and Wesley: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-5.html
- **A caution.** Constable notes many Palestinian Jews also had Greek names. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Another view of the choice.** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary thinks the church chose Hellenists to avoid seeming to favour the Hebrew widows, not to serve Hellenists only. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-5.html
- **Nicolas.** Gill mentions the view that the Nicolaitans of Revelation came from him, but also the view that they only borrowed his name. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-5.html Constable calls the link questionable. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Difference: were they "deacons"?**
  - Reformed (R.C. Sproul, Ligonier): the diaconate was founded here. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/apostles-and-deacons
  - Guzik: the word "deacon" isn't used, but most see them as the first deacons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
  - GotQuestions: they were forerunners of the later formal office. https://www.gotquestions.org/Prochorus-in-the-Bible.html
  - Constable: they were a stage in the development of the office. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
  - MacArthur (GTY): he rejects the deacon reading. The same Greek word is used for the apostles' own ministry in v. 4, and Stephen preached and Philip evangelised, so the seven were closer to elders. https://www.gty.org/articles/451020/answering-the-key-questions-about-deacons-booklet
- **Catholic view.** Constant church tradition says this is where the diaconate began; Irenaeus calls Stephen the first deacon. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Protestant commentators often object. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04647c.htm
- **Orthodox view.** Stephen is called "Archdeacon" because he was the eldest of the seven deacons. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives?q=Martyr
- **Legends.** Ellicott records a tradition that Stephen and Philip were among the Seventy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-5.html The Catholic Encyclopedia doubts a similar claim. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/stephen-martyr-saint

**v. 6**
- **Service is spiritual work.** Guzik: laying hands on them showed that practical service is spiritual service, since the same Greek word is used in vv. 1 and 4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **Difference: what did the laying on of hands do?**
  - Barnes: it gave no power. It showed their authority came from the apostles, and ordination has always been done this way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/6-6.htm
  - Calvin: a sign of consecration showing they were offered to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-6.html
  - Constable: a commissioning for a task, not formal ordination, which came later. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
  - Coffman: the apostles gave the seven miraculous powers (compare v. 8 and 8:18). He says calling it a mere ceremony is incorrect. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-6.html
  - Ellicott: this is the first time the act appears in the New Testament. It has lasted in the church in confirmation and ordination. https://biblehub.com/acts/6-6.htm
  - Clarke: he links it to Church of England deacons, ordained by a bishop and able to preach. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/acts-6.html
  - Catholic view: the Apostolic Constitutions pray for a new deacon to be filled "as Thou didst fill Stephen." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04647c.htm

**v. 7**
- **A progress report.** Constable: this is one of Luke's summaries that close each section of Acts. He also cites an estimate of about 2,000 priests in Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Which priests.** Constable cites F.F. Bruce: these were ordinary priests, not the wealthy chief-priestly families who opposed the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Ellicott.** No priest is named as following Jesus, and none had been converted before this. He connects the change with Stephen's new teaching. https://biblehub.com/acts/6-7.htm
- **Wesley.** The word grew once the hindrances were removed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/acts-6.html
- **Guzik.** Satan's attempt to divide the church failed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/

**v. 8**
- **"Faith" or "grace."** Guzik notes the manuscripts differ here but the meaning is much the same. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **Miracles.** Constable: Stephen's miracles seem unconnected to his appointment, and Jesus and the Twelve weren't the only ones who did miracles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html A NET note quoted by bible.org says Stephen is the first non-apostle described with the same words as the apostles. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-6-9

**v. 9**
- **The Freedmen.** Constable (citing Marshall) and the Catholic Encyclopedia say they were probably Jews, or their descendants, taken prisoner by Pompey and later freed. Constable thinks one synagogue is meant, not several. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html ; https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14286b.htm
- **Saul?** Because of the mention of Cilicia, Saul of Tarsus may have attended. Guzik (citing Lovett): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/ Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Synagogue preaching.** Constable: this is the first time Acts shows the gospel preached in a synagogue. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html

**v. 10**
- **The source of his wisdom.** Guzik credits the Spirit, not Stephen's own skill. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/ Constable links this to Jesus' promise in Luke 21:15 and calls Stephen a forerunner of later defenders of the faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html

**v. 11**
- **Lies after losing.** Guzik: having lost the debate, the opponents turned to secret lies. He suggests Luke may have learned the details from Saul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **Meaning of blasphemy.** Constable: at that time Jews defined blasphemy as any defiant sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html

**v. 12**
- **Persecution widens.** Constable: Stephen's arrest mirrors those of Jesus and the apostles, and now ordinary Christians are persecuted too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Violence.** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the Greek verb implies he was seized with some force. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14286b.htm

**vv. 13–14**
- **True ideas, twisted.** Constable, citing Longenecker: the charge was false less because it was invented than because it twisted what Stephen meant, much like the charge against Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **A distorted truth.** Guzik: the charges reflected Stephen's true message that Jesus surpasses the temple and the law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **A bolder reading.** The ISBE (via NET Bible's dictionary) says Stephen actually taught that the temple and the law were passing away, making him a forerunner of Paul. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Stephen

**v. 15**
- **What the "angel" face was.** Commentators split between calm composure and real supernatural light:
  - Calvin: his expression at that moment, not his natural face. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/6-15.html
  - Matthew Henry: perhaps just a cheerful face with no fear or anger. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_006.cfm
  - Pulpit Commentary: lit with divine radiance. https://biblehub.com/acts/6-15.htm
  - Gill: calm innocence that ought to have counted as God clearing him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/6-15.htm
  - Guzik: not a soft painted look, but peace and confidence, like the glory Moses reflected. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-6/
- **The Moses link.** Constable: the council should have seen Stephen as like Moses, not against him, and as a messenger bringing new revelation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-6.html
- **Where Luke heard it.** Ellicott traces the detail to the impression it made on Paul, who passed it to Luke. https://biblehub.com/acts/6-15.htm
